entries.title: The Chinese Philosopher Americans Can’t Stop Fighting About
entries.summary: Yiyang Zhuge was already an intellectual celebrity in China. Her viral interview with Christopher Nolan made her famous in the US—and quickly turned her into a political Rorschach test.
entries.content:
Yiyang Zhuge learned last week that when you go extremely viral, the people you have been following for years suddenly start following you back. Zhuge logged onto X and found that a string of famous professors and scholars were in her list of new followers. A PhD candidate in political philosophy at Boston College, Zhuge had previously only lurked on X to keep up with the latest debates and gossip in academia. The vast majority of her social media activity happens on the Chinese internet, where she goes by the alias Zhong Shu and hosts a popular podcast with hundreds of thousands of loyal listeners.

Late last month, Zhuge, who is in her late twenties, interviewed Christopher Nolan, one of the most influential directors in Hollywood, who was in Beijing promoting The Odyssey. Rather than asking about celebrities or Hollywood, Zhuge posed a series of deeply philosophical questions to Nolan about the Christianization of Greek philosophy and how to portray heroes in films. The first thing she asked: “Are you a bard for a civilization at dusk?”

Nolan was visibly impressed by Zhuge. After the interview was published in China, Geoff Keighley, a video game journalist and the son of Nolan’s longtime friend David Keighley, shared the interview on X, calling it “a great listen.” Keighley’s video has been watched over 18 million times, and when Zhuge later posted the interview on her own X account, it racked up another 6.9 million views.

For the first time, Zhuge had become the main character of the English-speaking internet. She was being praised, mocked, criticized, and defended all at the same time. Many people said it was the best interview Nolan has done for The Odyssey, while the National Review called it a “CCP hostage video.” But everyone ultimately wanted to know the same thing: Who was this young Chinese woman with a bob haircut talking about the decline of civilizations?

While almost no one in the West knows her name, Zhuge is already one of the most prominent young intellectuals in China and has been interviewed by many of the country’s cultural elite. She was featured in Vogue China as an example of a successful woman in her twenties and frequently shares yoga and fitness tips to her 360,000 fans on the Chinese social media platform Xiaohongshu.

When I spoke to Zhuge this week, she framed her success as being born out of personal tragedy. “I was going through an adulterous divorce in which my ex-husband sued me and I accumulated a lot of legal debt,” she says. “I felt discouraged in the English-speaking academia because of certain personal experiences related to that personal tragedy, so I turned my attention back to the Chinese-speaking world to build a career there and pay off my debt.”

When I started digging into Zhuge’s career, I was shocked by her level of productivity. Aside from publishing philosophy translations and writing articles for Chinese media outlets, she has recorded more than 360 episodes of her podcast Monologues of a Committed Observer in just the last three years. That’s an average of one new episode every three days. Most of the time, she just monologues about political science concepts for a half an hour, seemingly unscripted. On XiaoyuzhouFM, the most popular podcast streaming platform in China, she has over 940,000 subscribers.

But despite her prolific posting, Zhuge claims she isn’t interested in being famous. “I have no attachment to fame and no desire to preserve it for its own sake,” she tells me. “What I want is enough freedom and time to build a life centered on thought. That life requires some money, but not very much.”

View From America

When Zhuge asked Nolan if he saw himself as “a bard for a civilization at dusk,” she says she didn’t have a particular civilization in mind.

She views the question instead as part of the long philosophical tradition of pondering the demise of value systems. “I was not primarily attempting to issue a verdict on the contemporary United States,” she says, but “people are free to interpret the phrase through current debates about American or Western decline.”

That’s certainly how many people on Western social media interpreted it. On X, YouTube, and Reddit, commenters lamented about how Western interviewers are seemingly unable to ask the same kind of rigorous questions to their subjects. Some wondered why a Chinese woman was the one to ask philosophical questions about Greece, while others asked if Western institutions are still teaching students humanities and the classics.

To be fair, Zhuge was educated in the Western system. She has been studying in the US since high school, lectured at Boston College and Brandeis University, and translated books by Hannah Arendt and Plutarch (an ancient Greek philosopher) into Chinese. She lives in Boston for most of the year. Her academic work draws on Straussianism, an influential school of conservative political philosophy that has shaped the thinking of people like Peter Thiel. Her fame in China, which earned her the opportunity to talk to Nolan in the first place, is mostly tied to the way she can succinctly explain the American political system, though some critics think her own conservative ideological leanings show up often in her work.

“She was trained in American conservatism, so the questions she asked really resonated with the US’s educated public,” says Chenchen Zhang, an associate professor in international relations at Durham University. When the familiar insecurities of American conservatives came out of the mouth of a Chinese woman, the audience instantly believed “this is how China views the Western civilization,” Zhang says.

The internet’s reaction to Zhuge’s interview reminds me of “Chinamaxxing,” the meme that persisted through the first half of 2026 on platforms like Instagram and TikTok. The trend was promoted mostly by left-leaning, Gen-Z Americans trying to numb their anxiety about America’s decline by deliberately endorsing China and Chinese culture. Now, right-leaning Americans are indulging in the same kinds of worries by fawning over Zhuge’s reverence for the classics. They are really two sides of the same coin.

Defending Herself

As the American right rushed to claim Zhuge as one of its own, the far left moved to distance itself from her. On X, @zei_squirrel, a prominent but anonymous progressive account with 346,000 followers, called her either “a deranged fanatical neocon Zionist lunatic” or a Chinese state-media psy-op, pointing to the fact that Zhuge follows several conservative figures.

Zhuge says she’s no stranger to people across the political spectrum being mad at her. “In China, I try very hard to remain above the fray of the mob rather than let public controversy determine what I think or discuss.” she says. “The labels may differ across countries, but the vulgar human impulse to sort people into political camps is universal.”

As for the anonymous account’s claim that she is a Zionist, Zhuge posted one rebuttal on X but says she won’t engage further. “An account that searches through someone’s following list for Jewish names is not conducting any meaningful analysis,” she says, “This mentality is one reason American online public life has become so polarized. People no longer examine arguments; they investigate affiliations.”

Still, this brief moment of virality has clearly shaken her. In her most recent podcast episode published on Thursday, Zhuge talked about how this was the first time she truly felt that she became the subject of public discourse. There’s a not-so-subtle hint of rage in her tone, and the audience seemed to notice it too. One commenter noted that she had forgotten to say her signature farewell message at the end. Instead, she ended the podcast episode by playing Beethoven’s Symphony No. 3, which the composer dedicated to heroes. “I would rather listen to how revolution collided with destiny in the ‘Eroica’ Symphony than a bunch of people in my notifications speculating who was my puppeteer pulling the strings,” she said.

This is an edition of Zeyi Yang and Louise Matsakis’ Made in China newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

entries.title: The 7 Best TV Shows to Stream This Month
entries.summary: Lanterns, Dark Matter, and the original Star Trek are just a few of the TV shows you should be watching right now.
entries.content:
The big screen is having a moment. Spider-Man: Brand New Day is breaking box office records, while Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey has people dusting off Homer for the first time since high school. But television is keeping pace with a slate of can’t-miss new releases and beloved old favorites that are worth revisiting.

While plenty of outlets will tell you what everyone is watching (see: Ted Lasso), that’s not our goal. As always, the TV shows we’re watching this month reflect the kinds of stories WIRED covers every day—shows that explore technology, science, politics, culture, and the sometimes unsettling ways they intersect.

From prestige dramas to absurd comedies and one truly groundbreaking sci-fi series, these are the TV shows we think are worth making time for this month.

Star Trek: The Original Series

On September 8, 1966, science fiction changed forever with the premiere of the original Star Trek TV series. In the 60 years since, Gene Roddenberry’s ahead-of-its-time tale of the USS Enterprise crew’s journeys into deep space has spawned dozens of films, TV series, and video games, plus hundreds of books and comics—not to mention a number of real-world tech innovations. The legendary series has also shaped pop culture in countless other ways, giving us everything from Vulcan salutes and Klingons to the Prime Directive and the immortal command to “beam me up.”

Whether you’re a lifelong Trekkie or a curious newcomer, there’s never been a better time to see where one of television’s most influential franchises began. Though it ran for just three seasons, Star Trek: The Original Series left an outsized legacy, breaking barriers with one of television’s first interracial kisses, featuring a remarkably diverse cast at the height of the Civil Rights Movement, and inspiring generations of scientists, engineers, and storytellers to imagine a more optimistic future. Sixty years later, its blend of adventure, social commentary, and boundless curiosity remains as compelling as ever. Best of all, Paramount+ is home to nearly every corner of the Star Trek universe, from the beautifully remastered original series to its many spinoffs and feature films. If you’re celebrating the franchise’s 60th anniversary, there’s no better place to boldly go back to where it all began.

Futurama

Following a decade-long hiatus, Futurama made a triumphant comeback in 2023, complete with gags about The Twilight Zone and “Momazon” drone deliveries. Created by Matt Groening and David X. Cohen, the animated sci-fi comedy is set in the 31st century and follows the employees of the Planet Express delivery company as they stumble through bizarre adventures, alien encounters, and laugh-out-loud takes on everything from AI to corporate greed.

On August 3, the series kicked off its 14th season, which delivers more of the razor-sharp tech satire and surprisingly thoughtful science that have long made it one of television’s smartest comedies.

President Curtis

This summer is a particularly ripe moment for fans of irreverent animated sci-fi, as it also brings President Curtis, a new spinoff set in the Rick and Morty universe. While Futurama looks ahead at the possibilities—and absurdities—of the distant future, President Curtis takes a stranger route, following President Andre Curtis (voiced by Emmy-winning baritone Keith David) and his eccentric staff as they navigate inter-dimensional diplomacy, paranormal investigations, and other bizarre crises. The 10-episode series, which premiered on July 26, airs new episodes each Sunday night on Adult Swim, which then drop on HBO Max on Monday.

Lanterns

DC is taking its Green Lanterns in a decidedly darker direction with Lanterns, a new series that trades traditional superhero spectacle for a cosmic murder mystery. Starring Kyle Chandler as Hal Jordan and Aaron Pierre as John Stewart, the series follows the two Lanterns as they investigate a mystery that stretches across Earth and beyond.

With Lost cocreator Damon Lindelof, True Detective producer Chris Mundy, and comic book writer Tom King behind the series, Lanterns—which arrives on August 16—brings a noir-inspired edge to one of DC’s most iconic franchises.

The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare

In the early morning hours of November 13, 2022, the city of Moscow, Idaho, changed forever when four University of Idaho students were killed in their off-campus home. The investigation that followed captivated the nation, as authorities worked to piece together what happened and identify a suspect in a horrifying quadruple murder that appeared to have no clear motive.

The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare chronicles the investigation through access to victims’ friends and families and police footage, while examining how digital evidence and forensic technology helped investigators unravel one of the most closely watched true crime cases in recent years.

Dark Matter

What if the life you’re living isn’t the one you were meant to have? That’s the question at the heart of Dark Matter, the sci-fi thriller based on Blake Crouch’s best-selling novel. Season one followed physicist Jason Dessen (Joel Edgerton), who is pulled into an alternate version of his life after being transported to a parallel reality.

Season two, which premieres on August 28, picks up with Dessen and his family attempting to build a quiet existence in a world that finally feels safe … until new threats force them back into the multiverse with the help of a mysterious device known as the Box. As the search for the Box continues, the series dives deeper into questions of identity, choice, and the endless possibilities of the paths we could have taken.

The Undeclared War

Four years after its debut, The Undeclared War is back with a chillingly timely premise: a cyberattack targeting a nation’s election system. The British thriller returns to the shadowy world of GCHQ (the UK’s intelligence, security, and cyber agency), where analysts battle digital threats that could have devastating real-world consequences.

Set in a post-pandemic 2024, the series follows a team of analysts racing to defend the country’s digital infrastructure as tensions with Russia escalate. With Shaun of the Dead star Simon Pegg starring as operations chief Danny Patrick, the new season, which arrives on August 27, explores how cyberwarfare has transformed the nature of modern espionage.

entries.title: Zohran Mamdani’s NYC Tech Team Is What DOGE Should Have Been
entries.summary: The mayor of New York City has assembled a crew of Silicon Valley and United States Digital Service veterans to overhaul city services with better software.
entries.content:
A go-kart track is an odd location to launch a tech initiative in the nation’s biggest city. Yet last month there was New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, zipping around the 900-foot oval at Coney Island’s Luna Park before stepping up to a podium to unveil a program called Public Interest Technology (PIT) Crews. Thus the go-kart theme.

PIT will consist of five “game-changing” teams that, Mamdani promised, will “raise the bar for what New Yorkers can expect from City Hall.” Working closely with city agencies, these small groups of engineers and designers will strive to change the hidebound and confusing tenor of current city services by using state-of-art skills to rapidly whip up specialized apps that solve real problems. “We want to transform how New Yorkers interact with the government,” said the mayor. “We want to raise expectations on what government can deliver, because we really can deliver.”

Do those words sound familiar? If you follow government tech, they might. Because Mamdani’s message could have fit quite comfortably in the pitch that Barack Obama’s chief technology officer, Todd Park, delivered in 2014 while recruiting tech talent for what would become the United States Digital Service. The USDS was an idealistic effort to bring top Silicon Valley talent into the executive branch to bypass the logjams caused by outdated and inefficient IT, by building great, user-centric software.

The agency somehow survived the first Trump administration and kept going through the Biden term. But in 2025, Elon Musk and his DOGE wrecking crew infiltrated the agency and pulled the plug on much of the useful stuff. (Now, with the National Design Service, the Trump administration is ostensibly trying to revive some of what it destroyed.)

Mamdani’s PIT crew initiative adopts much of the original USDS ethos, with a timely twist: It embraces Silicon Valley expertise while taking a skeptical, almost adversarial, stance toward Big Tech itself. The combination of mayoral charisma and a chance to make software that doesn’t serve advertisers, the military, or the pocketbooks of centibillionaires makes the Mamdani team an attractive, high-status, mid-career change of pace for some techies. Suddenly, one of the sexiest places in geekdom is the Brooklyn headquarters of New York City’s Office of Technology and Innovation.

Mamdani’s transition team set the stage for an urban, democratic-socialist-adjacent, USDS-style tech squad when it tapped Lisa Gelobter for the city’s chief technology officer job. Gelobter’s résumé includes stints at big companies and startups, but the standout item was her post at the United States Digital Service, where she was embedded in the Department of Education. She led the effort to create a College Scorecard that focused on nuts-and-bolts criteria like costs and graduation rates. To this day, she gets misty when recalling her Washington experience; she even remembers what she was wearing when the USDS team took a group picture with Obama just before he left office.

“I’m really excited about trying to recapture that essence, that energy here,” she says. Her budget for the program is $5.24 million, with an additional $2 million grant from the Rockefeller Foundation, which will fund one of the crews.

Gelobter says she brings an engineering mindset to New York City government. “I know how to build software,” she says. “I know how to run a technology organization from a technology perspective.” It’s also a cultural thing for her. “I’m wearing jeans to work—not because I don’t look great in a suit, but it’s a statement, right?” she says. (The same norm-breaking happened in the USDS, which had to overcome objections from bureaucrats who didn’t want to meet with anyone wearing a hoodie.) Naturally, the two people Gelobter hired to run the PIT crew program are also USDS veterans, Luke Farrell and Maya Israni.

The projects Gelobter and her team choose to tackle will set a tone for the way the government works under a mayor whose future depends on how well he manages his city. “Without technology, policy is just words written on a piece of paper,” says Gelobter. Seen that way, the PIT crews are essentially Mamdani’s symbolic stand-ins in his fight against self-interested consultants and inefficient contractors. They will make their case by actually building things, in frantic 12-week sprints.

On its face, the first project of the PIT crew seems nonintuitive. The mission is to implement a pet mayoral project: click-to-cancel. On July 10, Mamdani announced this regulation, which penalizes companies that make it difficult to cancel subscriptions or ongoing payments. The rule takes effect on October 1, which is the exact date that the PIT crew plans to launch software that empowers citizens to blow the whistle on services that force people to go through hoops to end the relationship. (Mamdami might be the first customer; on Coney Island he admitted, “I am currently subscribed to something I don’t even know my login for, but they have my credit card information, and I don’t know how to cancel it.”)

The city hasn’t yet announced what the other four PIT crews will work on. My guess is that they will concentrate on more nuts-and-boltsy city services, and at least one will address the housing problem—but it’s telling that this first choice provides a way for ordinary people to stand up to bullying corporations. “It will show that we can directly affect people’s lives. It’s supposed to save, like, $160 million for New Yorkers,” says Gelobter. The project, she confirms, was a “mayoral priority.”

It’s perfect Mamdani branding. Even though much of Hizzoner’s personal tech surge is based on the USDS playbook, the conditions in 2026 are considerably different than they were in 2014. Back then, most people saw Silicon Valley as an enviable font of innovation, gumption, and high standards. The Obama-ites wanted to reflect Silicon Valley’s glory. These days, Big Tech is seen as an oppressive force, especially by progressive politicians and young people. So the choice sends a message that Mamdani’s version of a geek squad can not only make services accessible, but could also check the impulses of oligarchs.

That message seems to be resonating among techies who want to do something other than develop AI that might decimate the labor force. Farrell says that in the first week after the city posted PIT crew job opportunities, over 3,000 people applied for the roughly 35 available slots, and résumés are still pouring in. A shocking number have come from people who currently hold high-salaried jobs in big tech companies. (The city jobs pay considerably less, with no equity.)

“We've heard from a lot of folks recently who are disillusioned with the private tech industry and maybe went into tech because they wanted to apply tech for good,” says Israni. If those people make it to PIT crews, they can indeed apply their skills for good. Or, at the least, for Mamdani.

This is an edition of Steven Levy’s Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

entries.title: Scientists Used AI to Create 16 New Viruses
entries.summary: The use of AI systems to create viruses opens up new possibilities for combating bacterial resistance. It also raises concerns about the pace at which technology is outstripping regulation.
entries.content:
For the first time, an artificial intelligence system has created a series of previously unknown viruses capable of infecting and eliminating certain types of bacteria. This breakthrough opens up new possibilities for combating bacterial resistance. However, it also raises concerns about the potential misuse of this technology to design biological weapons.

For several years now, scientists have been able to synthesize viruses from scratch; these are typically used to develop and evaluate antiviral drugs and vaccines, as well as to expand our understanding of how these microorganisms behave. However, the production of these viral genomes has primarily relied on replicating previously known pathogens or variants.

In contrast, a new study conducted by scientists at Stanford University and the Arc Institute succeeded in having an AI design simple, functional, and previously unseen viruses based on information contained in the genetic sequences of millions of animals, plants, microbes, bacteria, and viruses found in nature

The researchers worked with bacteriophages—microorganisms characterized by relatively small genomes, which are relatively easy to synthesize and manipulate under controlled conditions. These viruses infect only bacteria, making them a tool with enormous biotechnological potential and a promising alternative to antibiotics for combating resistant bacterial infections.

The creation of these entirely new viruses was based on Evo 1 and Evo 2, foundational AI models developed for computational biology applications. Both algorithms were trained on millions of genomes from all domains of life, with the goal of identifying and learning complex evolutionary patterns, including how genes are typically organized, which sequences are conserved, and the biological constraints that allow an organism to remain functional.

The experimental design used the bacteriophage Phi X-174—which is capable of infecting the bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli)—as a reference. The goal was not to reproduce this virus, but rather to use it solely as a guide for the algorithms to generate thousands of completely new genomes with a genetic architecture compatible with infecting E. coli.

In other words, the viruses derived from the genomes created by the AI retained the functional organization essential for recognizing the bacterium, inserting their DNA, replicating it, producing new viral particles, and assembling them correctly. However, the specific DNA sequences differed considerably from those observed in naturally occurring bacteriophages.

16 New Viruses Created Using AI

The scientists then evaluated the AI-generated genomes to select those most likely to be functional, taking into account factors such as gene organization, the presence of regulatory elements, and other criteria inspired by the biology of the Phi X-174 bacteriophage.

This selection resulted in a sample of 300 genomes, which were artificially synthesized, molecule by molecule, in the laboratory. They were then introduced into E. coli bacteria to test whether they were capable of producing functional viruses.

Of the 300 synthesized genomes, only 16 gave rise to fully functional bacteriophages, featuring previously unpublished sequences, different genes, new regulatory elements, and even varying genome sizes. The behavior of these viruses also varied: While some infected the bacteria more quickly, others exhibited different abilities to replicate.

The research, published this week in the journal Science, also evaluated the ability of AI-generated bacteriophages to combat resistant bacteria. The experiment involved exposing a mixture of AI-designed phages and a mixture of natural phages similar to Phi X-174 to strains of E. coli that had already developed resistance to that virus.

The results showed that the AI-generated viruses were able to rapidly overcome bacterial resistance and establish infection. According to the authors, this finding demonstrates “a path toward artificial intelligence–generated phage therapies against rapidly evolving bacterial pathogens.”

The Two Sides of the Milestone

The discovery opens up new possibilities for tackling the growing problem of bacterial resistance. According to the researchers, this approach could facilitate the development of personalized treatments capable of evolving at nearly the same rate as the pathogens themselves.

Although this milestone represents a significant advance for molecular biomedicine, it also raises concerns about the potential malicious use of this technology to develop, for example, new diseases, highly toxic substances, or pathogens capable of triggering a new pandemic.

Moritz Hanke, a researcher at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, argues that there are currently no safeguards capable of effectively preventing the creation of a lethal virus with the help of AI, telling The New York Times that there is “a huge disconnect” between the speed at which science and technology are advancing and the development of effective regulatory frameworks.

The debate surrounding these risks is not new. Three years ago, a study by the Rand Corporation warned that the most advanced AI systems at the time had the capacity to refine the planning and execution of attacks using biological weapons. Now, with the rapid development of this technology, fears are growing that such capabilities will become even greater and more sophisticated.

The nonprofit organization also warned that the speed at which AI systems evolve often outpaces governments’ capacity for regulatory oversight.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

entries.title: Best Webcams (2026): My Honest Take After Testing the Best
entries.summary: I tested the best webcams across various prices to find the top option. Here’s what I learned.
entries.content:
It's difficult to measure the quality of the best webcams without evaluating them side by side. Every webcam I've ever tested handles light differently, and subtle variations in a room—like the location of your windows and the colors of your walls—can change your perception of a webcam’s capabilities.

So, when given the task of declaring one webcam winner, I realized I really needed to test all of them at the same time under the exact same lighting conditions. So, that's what I did. After many rounds of testing and using these webcams in my daily life, which just happens to include a very poorly lit home office, I came across a few gems that stood out from the rest.

Want more home-office recommendations? Check out our guide to the Best Printer for Every Home Office Need, the Best Standing Desks, and the Best Office Chairs.

Updated August 2026: I've added testing information about the Dell Pro 5 and Dell Pro 7 webcams. I've also added new photos to some existing recommended products.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

The Single Best Webcam

After testing more than 15 webcams, I found a clear winner for the best image quality, microphone, and design: the Insta360 Link 2C Pro ($200). It's remarkably compact and light, allowing it to work just as well on a laptop as on a monitor. That flexibility alone lends the webcam a uniquely practical design that most other webcams can't compete with. The Logitech MX Brio (my previous pick for best overall webcam) is almost three times heavier.

The Insta360 Link 2C Pro magnetizes to its strong aluminum mount, and I never worried about it falling back, even with the weight of the USB-C cable pulling on it. This also makes its panning adjustments super-smooth. It's surprising how many webcams struggle with this very simple motion, but it’s perhaps the result of many mounts being plastic—including the Logitech MX Brio. Because the Insta360 is magnetic, it can also stick to any other metal surface, which can be convenient if you're looking to shoot from a different angle.

In terms of image quality, no webcam at this price delivers lowlight performance on par with the Insta360 2C Pro. Right out of the box, without even tweaking any settings, I was impressed by its ability to handle harsh light. Like all the cameras, I tested it in some poor conditions, including under overhead office lighting and being backlit. The webcam handled these scenarios better than its competitors. It avoided blowing out the highlights and could deliver as much detail in the image as possible, even compared to more expensive webcams, like the Obsbot Tiny 3 ($349).

I also noticed its very natural image-processing contrast compared to options like the Logitech MX Brio, which tended to crush blacks. Under better lighting, the sharpness of the image really stood out. Thanks to that large 1/1.3-inch CMOS sensor, objects in the background fall out of focus in a natural bokeh effect. It mimics the look of a DLSR better than any camera I tested. Other webcams look flat by comparison.

It's not perfect—no webcam is. Sometimes there's a bit too much processing and smoothing for my taste, especially in some of the details around the face. And out of the box, the colors skew a bit cool. The easy-to-use software makes adjusting these issues easy, but it's something to be aware of nonetheless. Hopefully, by now, you'll be convinced that there's little reason to buy the Logitech MX Brio over the Insta360 2C Pro. Logitech has a lot of brand equity in the world of webcams, but considering both models retail for $200, Insta360 definitely has the superior product.

The standard Insta360 Link 2C ($150) is also a strong option. It's $50 cheaper, with a slightly smaller sensor and narrower aperture, resulting in worse low-light performance. I noticed that it introduced more noise, especially in areas of high contrast, such as along my hairline. But let's be real: Though you can hunt down the differences between these two webcams, the standard Link 2C still punches above its weight for the price.

One of the biggest disadvantages of the non-Pro model, though, is in microphone quality. The Insta360 2C is more in line with other webcams I tested. It uses just a single microphone and lacks the ability to pick up the deeper frequencies in my voice, whereas the 2C Pro uses a dual-microphone beam-forming system that does a far better job capturing the fuller spectrum. I still think that the Insta360 Link 2C is one of the best options at around $150, though, handily beating out models like the Razer Kiyo V2 and Logitech Brio 4K.

Cheap Webcams That Get the Job Done

Proceed very carefully with the following recommendations. That's especially true if you are working from a laptop with a built-in camera or already have a decent webcam. In general, I suggest dishing out some extra cash for one of the more premium options listed above, or buying a light to help your existing camera work better. Even a simple lighting accessory, like the $70 Logitech Litra Glow, will dramatically improve the quality of your video calls more effectively than buying a budget webcam.

That said, if you're using an external monitor and need a budget-friendly webcam to pair with it, there are a couple of decent options to consider. The Anker PowerConf C200 ($66) is the best of the bunch that I've tested. It has issues, such as the built-in mount, which can't swivel left or right. It also doesn't grip the monitor as effectively as I'd want. While the 5-megapixel camera can't compare with the larger sensors in the more premium webcams, the image quality is decent enough, especially if your room has nice light and you don't mind tweaking the picture quality in the software.

I'd also hesitantly recommend the Logitech Brio 300 ($60). Like the C200, it has a number of deficiencies. On this model, those drawbacks include an unappealing sticky pad built into the integrated mount and the built-in cable. The microphone also won't be much of an upgrade over the ones built into MacBooks, though it's still better than built-in mics on many of the Windows laptops I've tested. I also don't like that the Brio 300 has a fixed 70-degree field-of-view, which gives it a smaller framing than all the other webcams I’ve tried.

That's a lot of complaints, I know. But if you just need something simple and “good enough,” the Logitech Brio 300 will do and certainly has better lowlight performance over an older option, like the Logitech C920. If you have decent lighting in your room, the Brio 300 will still be an upgrade over your laptop's webcam in terms of image quality.

For options that ring up for something between the $60 of my budget picks and the $150 of my top picks, check the honorable mentions below. That said, I haven't encountered a $100-range webcam that actually feels like it's worth the money—or the extra money beyond a budget recommendation. I'm curious if the Anker AnkerWerk C310 $100—the 4K upgrade over the C200 from a few years ago—will change my mind when I test it soon. It comes in right at $100 and has a larger 1/2.5-inch sensor.

The Best PTZ Webcams

PTZ, also known as pan-tilt-zoom webcams, are far more versatile than a standard webcam. Essentially, the camera sits on a gimbal and can follow you around a room using face-tracking technology. These cameras can pan far to the left or right, tilt up and down, and use a digital zoom. That's a pretty advanced feature set, and likely not the kind of thing most people shopping for a webcam really need. But if you happen to use your webcam for streaming, giving presentations, teaching courses, or really anything else that involves staying on camera while moving about your room, you could probably benefit from one. Even if you don't need one, you'll probably get a kick out of just experimenting with its capabilities.

There are a couple of impressive PTZ options, but the best is the Obsbot Tiny 3 ($349), which is also the most expensive webcam I tested. While its price tag is likely more than what most people want to spend on a webcam, the camera did produce the overall best color accuracy, replicating real-life color without looking overprocessed. Its image quality is better than any other webcam I tested—even beyond what the Insta360 cameras can do. I still prefer the lowlight performance of the Insta360 cameras, but the Obsbot Tiny 3's colors are more natural. It can even shoot in 120 frames per second in 1080p, though I'm not sure quite what the use case is for that.

Obsbot has a cheaper version as well, the Obsbot Tiny 3 Lite ($199), which very well may be the PTZ webcam that most people should buy, in light of the lower price. It's a minor step down in image quality, as it uses a small camera sensor. The most notable trade-offs, though, are that you don't get as much of that natural background blur, and the lowlight performance isn't as strong. But it's one of the most affordable ways to get the PTZ features without too much of a downgrade in quality. (And really, the PTZ features are why you’d buy these cameras anyway.)

In its latest release, Obsbot has introduced lots of interesting new ways to use AI to control the gimbal, like tracking objects, following your voice, and giving you a few audio modes for specific use cases. There's even a feature that allows you to use preset voice commands to control the gimbal, such as choosing between preset angles or zooming in. All of the previous (and extensive) software features are still around, too. Among others, those features include setup for customizable preset angles, desk mode, and multiple head-tracking speeds. There's tons to play around with, making PTZ cameras fun in addition to being useful.

If you like the design of the Insta360, though, the company has a PTZ version of the Link 2C Pro that I recommended above. The Insta360 Link 2 Pro ($249) has the exact same picture and microphone quality as the 2C, but with the additional capability of being able to pan, tilt, and zoom. (There's also a cheaper model, the Insta360 Link 2 ($196).) The main benefit it has over the Obsbot Tiny 3 is that it's a full $100 cheaper. That's significant, even if the color accuracy isn't quite as strong on the more affordable model. For what it's worth, I preferred the way Link 2 Pro handled the lowlight scenarios over the Obsbot Tiny 3. The Tiny 3 was definitely overexposed right out of the box.

Though the Insta360 Link 2 Pro is not quite as full-featured as the Obsbot cameras in terms of AI trickery, I do like that you can control the gimbal using your phone to make adjustments. Instead of having to rely solely on the desktop software or voice commands, the Insta360 cameras let you quickly pull up controls in a browser on your phone after scanning the QR code, which is super handy.

Before You Buy, Try Using Your Smartphone

You may not need a dedicated webcam at all. It's actually really easy to use your smartphone's cameras as a webcam instead. In fact, your smartphone is usually far superior to a webcam. Recent iPhones, for example, have a feature called Continuity Camera, which works with certain MacBooks and allows you to wirelessly use the iPhone's camera as a webcam. Apple even sells a Belkin mount ($30) that lets you hang your iPhone off the top of your MacBook or external monitor for the full effect.

Google Pixel phones also now feature wired webcam support. To use it, plug in a Pixel to your computer and choose the webcam option you want. You'll just need a tripod to keep it propped up; something like this Joby GripTight will do the job.

Don't have either of these smartphones? Don't fret. We have a full guide on How to Use Your Smartphone as a Webcam, complete with multiple methods, no matter which PC or phone you own. We also have a guide for setting up a professional camera as a webcam.

How to Improve Your Webcam

An easy way to improve your existing webcam is to add a light source. Webcams have small camera sensors, so they often need a lot of light to deliver good results. One that I’d recommend is the Lume Cube Mini LED Panel ($70). It’s simple to use, allowing you to adjust the brightness and the color temperature to match your room's lighting. It can either use battery power, or you can leave it plugged in via the USB-C cable to run for however long you want. Its two quarter-inch threads mean you can use any tripod or light stand to mount it on your desk. It also comes with a diffuser to soften the light when it illuminates your face. For more lighting options, check our Home Video Gear guide.

Webcams also typically have poor microphones. The higher-end webcams typically have better microphones that’ll do the job, but you'll still probably sound tinny. If you own a MacBook Pro, you may find that its mics actually sound better than the built-in mic in the webcam. Videoconferencing apps let you choose which mic you want to use, so just because you have a separate webcam doesn't mean you have to use its built-in mic.

Another option is to upgrade to a USB mic like the Logitech Blue Yeti Nano USB Mic ($120). Logitech microphones are the standard-bearers in the world of USB microphones; the Nano packs everything most people need, but in a smaller footprint. Plug it into your computer, and once you choose this mic in your video-calling settings as the default, you'll immediately start hearing compliments from people on the other end. Read our Best USB Mics guide for more details.

Is a 4K Webcam Worth It?

Most videoconferencing software cap the resolution at 1080p for bandwidth purposes, so a 4K webcam may not be necessary at all. However, almost all 4K webcams come with software that lets you crop in or reframe the image, allowing you to, say, move something in the background of your home office out of frame. Most importantly, most 4K webcams will produce better image quality in general. They're more expensive, but if you can afford one, it’ll deliver the best-looking feed for video calls.

It's also important to consider that 4K webcams often shoot at 30 frames per second, but usually also offer 1080p at 60 frames per second. I should note, though, that while 4K cameras often can shoot in 1080p, they are being downsampled and can sometimes result in artifacts or messy details.

Understanding Megapixels, Resolutions, and Sensors

A webcam’s picture quality matters most, but there are a number of camera specs that play into it. For starters, what we usually just call “resolution” is the pixel count of the final image, usually either 1080p, 1440p, or 4K. The sharpness of this final image is important, but it doesn't alone tell the whole story on image quality.

The camera sensor itself also has a resolution, usually referred to in megapixels, which is just the total number of pixels (rather than resolution, which uses a width by height dimension). More megapixels can produce higher-quality images, but the physical size of the sensor is also important. A larger sensor with a lower megapixel count will often result in better images. Sensors also often have confusing labels attached to them. But, as a guiding principle, the bigger sensor, the better. So, a 1/1.3-inch sensor (which is as large as webcam sensors get right now) is better than a 1/2-inch sensor.

There are, of course, other important parts of cameras, such as the aperture of the lens, which controls how much light the camera captures and can affect lowlight performance. Most webcams have an aperture of f/2.0, but some models that have better lowlight performance, like the Insta360 Link 2C Pro, have a wider f/1.9 aperture.

Lastly, the image processing has a lot to do with the final quality of the image. Webcams these days use lots of AI-based image processing to sharpen and balance the image around your face, including filtering out noise and smoothing out skin tone. Most of us want this to look as natural as possible, and there's no question that some webcams are too heavy-handed.

Do Webcams Work With Laptops?

Yes, most webcams work just fine with laptops. Most laptops don't high-quality internal webcams, so any one of these webcams should improve the image quality. Most of the mounts that come with these webcams, however, are designed for external monitors. I've found that while that most can rest on a laptop lid just fine, they're not tightly secured as they would be on an external monitor. But obviously, the smaller the camera the better for a laptop, which is why the Insta360 cameras work well.

Other Good Webcams I Tested

Dell Pro 5 for $120: Not everyone wants to spend $150 or $200 on a webcam, and there's a surprising lack of good options closer to $100. The Dell Pro 5 is decent, and it comes with Windows Hello. It's not 4K (up to 1440p instead), but image quality is nice enough for the price, especially if you're willing to make some tweaks to the brightness and contrast. The magnetic mount is nice too, but it's unfortunate that it comes with a built-in USB-A cable rather than a detachable one.

YoloCam S3 for $199: I’ve seen this one promoted all over social media, and I’m happy to report that I like its ability to easily shoot in portrait. Just flip it around on its magnetic stand, and you're instantly shooting social media-ready content. Its lowlight performance isn't as strong as other options at this price, however, and it was buggy out of the box when I tested across multiple devices. But it's still one of the strongest competitor to the Insta360 Link 2C Pro of anything I tested.

Razer Kiyo V2 for $113: I love the click of the physical shutter closing, but the lowlight performance was a bit disappointing, especially for how large of a device this is. The new white colorway that I tested is pretty, though, and for the price, the image quality isn't bad. The Razer Kiyo Pro Ultra that creates the most natural bokeh effect is also in this line, but it also costs $400.

Obsbot Meet 2 for $129: This is, by far, the smallest and lightest webcam I tested, making it a solid option for laptop users. That compact size also means a smaller sensor, though lowlight performance wasn't its strong suit. I'd still take this over the Logitech Brio 500 (which is currently out of stock). There's also the 1080p Obsbot Meet SE ($69) that I plan to test in the future as a midrange option.

Logitech MX Brio for $200: It produces decent 4K image quality, but for the price, I prefer the Insta360 Link 2C Pro's image processing, lowlight performance, and microphone quality.

Don’t Bother With These Webcams

Dell Pro 7 for $200: This one didn't cut it for the price. I went in with high hopes, given the specs and hardware inside. But comparing this device to something like the Insta360 Link 2C Pro (or even Link 2C) yields results that are night and day in terms of image quality, microphone clarity, and focus speed.

Logitech C920 for $68: It's hard to believe this old webcam is still being sold and purchased, despite being 14 years old. It was the go-to webcam for many, many years, but it's not worth buying in 2026. You'll also see variants of it out there, such as the C920x, C920S, and C920e, but none are meaningful improvements on the basic image quality.

Emeet SmartCam S800 for $70: Getting a 4K resolution at this price is tempting, but the out-of-the-box color accuracy is rough, producing an overly green image. This can be tweaked in the software, but I also found that it has an over-sharpened effect that gave it a fake digital effect. I just couldn't get this to look how I wanted.

Logitech 4K Brio for $170: It's too expensive for the quality, especially with how oversaturated the colors look. It is, however, one of the only webcams that supports Windows Hello facial authentication.

Emeet Pixy for $90: This PTZ webcam is undeniably cute, resembling a little robot friend hanging out on your monitor. It actually uses two cameras to speed up autofocus and support AI features. The autofocus is fast, but I didn't notice it functioning any quicker than other high-end cameras. The lowlight performance really suffers, though, the microphone is awful, and it's a far larger PTZ webcam than the others on the list.

Logitech Brio 500 for $130: This isn't a bad webcam per se, but it's just not worth $130. I don't like the integrated mount or cable, and the lowlight performance can't compete. You can spend even more on the Brio 505, which is the same camera, except it comes with a removable USB-C cable.

entries.title: The 5 Best Laptop Power Banks I've Personally Tested (2026)
entries.summary: These powerful, high-capacity portable batteries are the best ones when laptop charging is a priority. All have at least 20,000 mAh, enough to charge most laptops twice.
entries.content:
Toss the right laptop power bank in your bag, and you'll never need to do that panicked run to the nearest outlet again. A hefty portable charger frees you to sit anywhere with your laptop and keep it running. Power banks with USB-C ports can charge phones and headphones as well, and I’ve tested more than 100 of them over the past few years. These powerful, high-capacity portable batteries are the best ones when laptop charging is a priority. For this guide, I considered power banks that are 20,000 mAh and up, enough to charge most laptops twice.

If you want some smaller portable chargers, check out my guide to the Best Power Banks or Best Qi2 and MagSafe Power Banks, or for more power, the Best Portable Power Stations.

Updated August 2026: I added power banks from ReelCharge and Pisen, removed some older devices, and updated prices.

Best Laptop Power Bank

Power bank manufacturers have made strides in pushing up potential charging rates in their high-capacity portable chargers. EcoFlow’s Rapid Pro X is a prime example, just edging out Anker’s Prime series below. Capable of delivering 300 watts, this power bank is close to the maximum capacity allowed on flights, and can charge a couple of laptops and phones at the same time via the three USB-C ports (140W, 65W, 65W) and a retractable USB-C cable (140W). It has a wee display showing remaining power as a percentage and the charging rate for each connected device. You can also check temperature and battery health, tweak the brightness and screen timeout, and even connect to your phone via the Ecoflow app (though most folks won’t need to).

The Rapid Pro offers a laundry list of charging capabilities (PD3.1, PPS, QC3.0, AFC, Apple2.4A, BC1.2, SCP, FCP, UFCS), but its greatest feature could be its super speedy recharge rate. Charge from a single USB-C input at 140 watts, and it takes an hour or so to fill, but you can plug in both at once to hit 80 percent from dead in under half an hour. Even better, Ecoflow’s dock can charge via the pogo pins on the bottom at 320 watts, enabling you to go from zero to 80 percent in just 20 minutes. You can fully charge it while you pack a bag. The Rapid Pro X comes with the 27,650 mAh model and the charging dock. Ecoflow also offers a 20,000-mAh, 230W Rapid Pro model ($140).

Specs
Ports: USB-C x 3, retractable USB-C cable
Capacity: 27,650 mAh
Charges: Most laptops one to two times
Wattage: 300 watts
Warranty: 2 years

Best Laptop Power Bank With a Dock

Anker introduced an innovative, high-wattage, high-capacity Prime Power Bank series a few years ago with an optional docking station for faster recharging via pogo pins on the bottom. This model is more compact and powerful than ever, offering 26,250 mAh at 300 watts across two USB-C ports and one USB-A, making it suitable for charging a couple of MacBooks and a smartphone at once. It also boasts a smart display and app control, and it comes with a 3.3-foot USB-C cable. Plug in both USB-C ports, and you can recharge at 250 watts to 80 percent from zero in 20 minutes.

All it's missing compared to my top pick is that retractable cable, but it's a handy extra to have. There are a few older models in the Prime series, including a smaller 20,100-mAh version ($150) that can output 220 watts and a 27,650-mAh model ($150) that’s bigger but capped at 250 watts. Anker's charging dock is a little nicer, more affordable than EcoFlow's, and easier to use with the Prime range.

Specs
Ports: USB-C x 2, USB-A
Capacity: 26,250 mAh
Charges: Most laptops one to two times
Wattage: 300 watts
Warranty: 2 years

Best Value Laptop Power Bank

You get an impressive range of features for your money with this laptop power bank from newcomer ReelCharge. The ReelPro (Model PWB3001) offers a generous 27,000-mAh capacity, has a built-in braided USB-C cable, and sports an informative display that shows precise battery stats. It’s a little light on ports, with just one USB-C and one USB-A, but both are rated at 100 watts, and the cable can deliver up to 140 watts. The combined maximum output of 200 watts is enough to charge a couple of laptops or your laptop and other devices.

Compared to my top picks, it is missing some fast-charging protocols for phones (it’s just Power Delivery for USB-C and Quick Charge for USB-A), and the power bank takes just over an hour to charge, as the input maxes out at 100 watts via the USB-C cable or port. ReelCharge is a new brand, so it’s a bit riskier as a purchase. But the company is offering a three-year warranty, and I’m impressed with how well the ReelPro works so far. I’ll keep testing to see how it holds up over time. ReelCharge also offers a 20,000-mAh model ($100) with a similar design.

Specs
Ports: USB-C x 1, USB-A x 1, retractable USB-C cable
Capacity: 27,000 mAh
Charges: Most laptops one to two times
Wattage: 200 watts
Warranty: 3 years

A Power Bank With Sci-Fi Styling

Long may this trend of sci-fi-styled portable chargers continue. The Aohi Starship looks like something you might find on the Nostromo, with a black and yellow design, three ports in one end, and a display to show remaining battery life as a percentage and wattage in and out. Information is in yellow, but the display is very dim (too dim to make out in direct sunlight). This power bank supports PD 3.1 and can deliver a chart-topping 240 watts for two devices via the two USB-C ports (140 watts and 100 watts), making it a good choice if you want to charge two laptops simultaneously.

You can fly with it in your carry-on, and there's a 140-watt 3.3-foot USB-C cable in the box. Aohi also offers a smaller, 25,200-mAh model ($140) that can deliver up to 100 watts via two USB-C ports or a bigger model capped at 140 watts. The larger, 40,000-mAh version ($190) will get you closer to two full charges, but it's a bit slower, and you can't take it on a plane.

Specs
Ports: USB-C x 2, USB-A
Capacity: 27,600 mAh (25,200 mAh or 40,000 mAh)
Charges: Most laptops one to two times
Wattage: 240 watts
Warranty: 18 months

More Power

If you're heading out for a weekend in the wilderness or a long road trip and want to keep your laptop ticking, this portable charger has a whopping 90,000-mAh capacity. You can charge it to 80 percent in an hour using the two fast USB-C ports, but it also has an XT60 input for a 100W solar panel (it took me several hours to fully charge this way) and a socket for charging from your car. It is heavy (6.17 pounds), but the tall form and carry handle make it easy to take with you, and Anker sells an optional shoulder strap for $30. You can connect the Anker app on your phone via Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, but you don’t need to, as the display shows the percentage remaining, watts in or out, and a time-remaining estimate.

This is too big to carry around day-to-day, and you can't fly with it, but if you're going off-grid for a few days, it's the highest-capacity portable charger you can realistically carry easily. It also has a lovely pop-up lantern with three brightness settings and a versatile array of ports. I have a separate Best Portable Power Stations guide with recommendations for anyone who needs even more power.

Specs
Ports: USB-C x 4, USB-A x 2
Capacity: 90,000 mAh
Charges: Most laptops up to four times
Wattage: 300 watts
Warranty: 2 years

Other Great Laptop Power Banks

Here are a few more tried and tested power banks for laptops that might be worth considering.

Pisen TP-D108 Power Bank for $50: With a 20,000-mAh capacity and a built-in USB-C cable capable of delivering up to 67 watts, this bargain power bank could be a handy laptop companion. It has a basic display showing remaining power as a percentage, along with one USB-C (67W) and one USB-A (22.5W) port. It supports a few fast-charging protocols (QC 3.0, PD 3.0, AFC, and FCP). It also has the CCC-certification mark required for domestic flights in China.

Anker Laptop Power Bank for $105: While this power bank is an excellent all-rounder and tops my best power banks guide, the 100-watt limit means it can’t charge your laptop as quickly as my other picks. If you don’t care about speed, it’s still a solid option, but sticking with Anker, some folks will prefer the Prime above, with a 300-watt maximum output, or the 737 below, because it can send or receive 140 watts from a single USB-C port.

Shargeek 170 Power Bank for $129: Perfect for lovers of translucent tech, this power bank has a 24,000-mAh capacity capable of charging most laptops once. It looks cool, with a smart display showing battery life as a percentage, time remaining, and the input or output in watts, and it supports Power Delivery 3.1, Quick Charge 4.0, and PPS, among other standards. While the total maximum output is 170 watts, you are limited to 140 watts from a single USB-C port.

Anker 737 Power Bank for $110: This is a versatile and reliable 24,000-mAh-capacity power bank that supports power delivery 3.1 and can send or receive up to 140 watts to charge laptops. You can charge it from zero within an hour. It’s relatively compact, but it weighs almost 1.4 pounds. The snazzy digital display shows the remaining battery percentage and stats, including the temperature, total output, cycles, and more. It fast-charged everything I tested it with, and you can charge three devices at once without a problem.

Ugreen 145W Power Bank for $65: Surprisingly compact for a 25,000-mAh battery, this weighs 1.1 pounds and has two USB-C ports and one USB-A port. Our former pick for tablets, the Ugreen, actually offers 145 watts, one USB-C port at 100W, and the other at 45W. There's a small LED readout on the side of the battery with the current charge state of the battery. I'd have liked to see some charging info on that screen as well, but that's a small quibble with what's an otherwise outstanding option if you need to keep your tablet or iPad charged up wherever you are.

Cuktech 15 Ultra for $79: With impressive build quality, including a nice grippy material on the underside and a handy display showing power output and input, this Cuktech (pronounced chook-tek) power bank boasts 20,000-mAh capacity, can charge two or three devices simultaneously at up to 165 watts, and supports many fast-charging protocols including PPS, QC, PD3.1, FCP, SCP, and MiPPS.

Laptop Power Bank FAQ

What Features Should I Look for in a Power Bank?

There are a few things worth thinking about when you’re shopping for a portable charger.

The capacity of a power bank is measured in milliampere-hours (mAh), but this can be a little misleading because the amount of power you get out depends on the cable you use, the device you're charging, and the charging method (Qi wireless charging is less efficient). You will never get the maximum capacity. We try to provide a minimum estimate of what you’ll get in terms of charges for a laptop battery.

The charging rate for devices like smartphones is measured in watts (W), but most power banks list the voltage (V) and the amperage (A). Thankfully, you can calculate the wattage yourself simply by multiplying the voltage and amperage. Unfortunately, getting that maximum rate also depends on your device, the standards it supports, and the charging cable you use. For best results match the charging speed across the power bank, cable, and laptop.

Your device will need pass-through support if you want to charge your power bank and use it to charge another device simultaneously. Many portable chargers support pass-through charging. Anker discontinued support for pass-through in some of its products because it found that differences between the output of the wall charger and the input of the device being charged can cause the power bank to cycle on and off rapidly and shorten its life. We would advise caution when using pass-through, as it can also cause portable chargers to heat up.

Can I Take a Power Bank on a Flight?

It’s safe to fly with a power bank, but there are two main restrictions to keep in mind when you board a flight: You must have the portable charger in your carry-on luggage (it cannot be checked), and it must not exceed 100 watt-hours (WH). If your power bank has a capacity larger than 27,000 mAh, you should check with the airline. Below that should not be a problem.

Some airlines have introduced stricter rules, so always check with your chosen airline before you travel. For example, some airlines prefer you not to use or charge power banks during a flight, some require power banks to be in your hand luggage under the seat in front of you and not in the overheads, and some limit the number of power banks you can have onboard.

How I Test Power Banks

I've been testing power banks for close to two decades, and my home office has stacks of ’em at any given moment. I test every portable charger that comes in for at least two weeks. I always check how many times it can fully charge my test laptop (currently a MacBook Air). I'll also try charging my Pixel 10 Pro XL, iPhone 16, and whatever else I have in. For this guide, I also tested with a Chromebook. I test how long it takes to recharge each empty power bank.

Aside from standard tests, I try to use the power banks in my everyday life, just to see how they feel, and my wife and kids often help out and share their opinions. For some of our top picks, I continue to test over months to get a sense of their reliability and durability, though it's not possible to do this for every device that lands on my desk. Beyond function, I take form and usability into account. I keep an eye on user reviews and consider the warranties and customer service of each manufacturer.

How Does WIRED Select Power Banks to be Reviewed?

I scan the latest releases to seek out worthy prospects, whether from an unknown new brand or an established favorite like Anker. I also get pitched many power banks every week. I sometimes reach out to these companies to ask for the product but never promise any kind of editorial coverage—that would be against WIRED's editorial policies. While WIRED usually earns affiliate revenue if you purchase a power bank using our link, this is not factored into the decision process when ranking.

There are too many power banks for me to test everything, so I tend to stick to reputable brands, but there's always room for something new if it has a compelling new feature or price, and I cover as many as I can. (Leave a comment or send me an email if you want me to test a power bank from a certain brand!) Once testing is complete, I typically donate power banks to a local charity. I try to hang on to some of our top picks for comparison purposes and to test their longevity.

entries.title: 3 Best Cheap Gaming Laptops (2026): Lenovo, MSI, Alienware
entries.summary: As gaming laptop prices continue to rise, it’s increasingly difficult to find affordable options that aren’t terrible. Here are your best options based on performance and cost.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

There was a time not so long ago when you could buy a decent gaming laptop for around $800. It wouldn't be pretty, but it could play modern games at decent frame rates and provided an entry point to PC gaming for a broader demographic.

These days, those same laptops cost $400 or $500 more. Meanwhile, the newer generation of entry-level gaming laptops has arrived, often offering similar performance for even more money—or by compromising the overall quality of the system. But there are a few standouts I've tested worth mentioning. And while it may not feel like the best time to buy a cheap gaming laptop, prices may only increase in the future.

For more laptop picks, check out our Best Cheap Laptops, Best Gaming Laptops, Best Windows Laptops, and Best Laptops guides. Make sure to read our comprehensive guide on How to Choose a Gaming Laptop.

Updated August 2026: I've reevaluated all the picks to reflect new prices and context. I've also added testing from the Alienware 15 and Lenovo LOQ 15 Essential Gen 11.
